walkthroughs.body_html:
Fundamentals Of Algorithms — a core area of A-Level Computer Science.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Fundamentals Of Algorithms brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Fundamentals Of Algorithms.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Dijkstra's shortest path algorithm is not guaranteed to work correctly when the graph contains:
options: More than ten vertices
Negative edge weights
Cycles of any kind
An odd number of edges

mcqs.q: Which data structures do depth-first and breadth-first traversal typically use?
options: DFS uses a queue; BFS uses a stack
Both use hash tables
DFS uses a stack; BFS uses a queue
Both use binary trees

mcqs.q: Binary search can only be applied to data that is:
options: Stored in a linked list
All numeric
Smaller than 100 items
Sorted into order

mcqs.q: The worst-case time complexity of merge sort is:
options: O(n log n)
O(log n)

mcqs.q: Can binary search be used on an unsorted list?
options: Yes - binary search sorts the list automatically as it searches.
Yes - DFS is shortest because stacks are faster than queues.
No - binary search relies on the list being sorted so it can discard half the items at each comparison; on unsorted data it can miss the target.
Yes - binary search works on any list because it checks the middle item.

mcqs.q: Does O(n^2) mean an algorithm is exactly twice as slow as an O(n) one?
options: Yes - the exponent 2 means it always takes twice as long.
Yes - binary search sorts the list automatically as it searches.
No - Big-O describes growth rate: doubling the input roughly quadruples the work for O(n^2) but only doubles it for O(n); the gap widens with input size.
Yes - O(n^2) algorithms always take two seconds per item.

mcqs.q: Does depth-first search always find the shortest path in an unweighted graph?
options: Yes - O(n^2) algorithms always take two seconds per item.
Yes - any traversal that reaches the target finds the shortest route.
No - DFS plunges down one path and may reach the target by a long route; breadth-first search, exploring level by level, finds the shortest path in an unweighted graph.
Yes - DFS is shortest because stacks are faster than queues.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Big-O notation”?
options: An algorithm that finds the shortest path from a start vertex to others in a weighted graph, requiring all edge weights to be non-negative.
A divide-and-conquer sort that splits a list into halves, sorts each half, then merges them, with O(n log n) time complexity.
Visiting every vertex of a graph systematically; breadth-first search explores level by level while depth-first search follows each path as far as possible.
A notation describing how an algorithm's time or space requirement grows with input size, ignoring constant factors and lower-order terms.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Tree traversal”?
options: A divide-and-conquer sort that splits a list into halves, sorts each half, then merges them, with O(n log n) time complexity.
Visiting every node of a tree in a defined order; pre-order, in-order and post-order traversals differ in when the root is visited.
A notation describing how an algorithm's time or space requirement grows with input size, ignoring constant factors and lower-order terms.
Visiting every vertex of a graph systematically; breadth-first search explores level by level while depth-first search follows each path as far as possible.
